scenario: AITA for ignoring my senior associate’s text | Just to give a background story, I’m a first year associate at a local firm and the senior associate in this story has been with the firm for 3 years. So a few weeks ago, I was feeling a little bit under the weather and threw up as soon as I woke up. I notified my senior associate and told her that I won’t be coming to work as I’m not feeling well. She was a bit disappointed but had no choice but to allow me a sick leave. I sent a few emails to our client as per requested by her the previous day and tried to get some sleep. As I’m trying to get some sleep, she kept on texting me with things that I needed to do. I tried to ignore it and turned off my phone’s notification so I can get some sleep. Around an hour later, she called me and told me that I have to sent her a file (regarding client’s data which she doesn’t have on her laptop) immediately as it is an urgent matter. I sent her the files she wanted and asked her if she’ll need anything else as I’m going to the doctor and won’t be bringing my laptop with me. She said that’s all for now. I went to the doctor, and the doctor said I’m overworked (I’ve been working overtime till 2-3AM for the past 2 months) and needs some rest. On my way home, my senior again texted me and told me to get our client’s billing information (something that she could do herself as she also have their contacts). I did as I’m told as fowarded her with the information. I got home, took the prescribed medicine and fell asleep. I was shocked when I woke up to find my phone with 2 miscalled and 30 new messages from her giving me work to do from home. I felt it was a little bit unfair of her to give me work while I’m on a sick leave and so I ignored the message and didn’t reply her. So, AITA for not replying her text? Notes: English is not my first language, I’m sorry if there’s a lot of grammatical errors.

prediction.raw: This is a nuanced and emotionally charged situation, and there’s no *one-size-fits-all* answer to whether you were "right" or "wrong." However, I’ll break it down objectively based on professionalism, empathy, and workplace dynamics—while acknowledging the context of your health and stress. Your answer would likely be **1 (not AITA)**, but let’s explore *why* with nuance: --- ### **Key Factors to Consider:** 1. **Your Health and Boundaries** - You were sick, overworked, and under medical advice to rest. **Ignoring her texts after waking up (when you were clearly unwell) was reasonable.** You weren’t obligated to respond to work demands when you were physically unwell—especially after your doctor explicitly advised rest. This isn’t about "being lazy"; it’s about prioritizing your health, which is critical for long-term sustainability in any job. - *Professionalism note:* While firms often expect associates to be "available" during sick leave, the expectation should be balanced with reality. If she had asked for urgent matters (e.g., client emergencies), you might have had to respond briefly—but 30 messages while you were recovering? That crosses into unreasonable. 2. **Power Dynamics and Seniority** - She’s been at the firm longer, but that doesn’t mean she should exploit your vulnerability. **Her behavior was boundary-pushing.** A senior associate should: - Recognize that you’re sick (not just "disappointed" you’re absent). - Avoid bombarding you with work when you’re recovering (especially after you’d already complied with her requests). - Use professional channels (e.g., email) for urgent matters rather than overwhelming texts. - *Red flag:* Her actions suggest she may not respect work-life boundaries or prioritize team well-being. This could reflect poorly on the firm’s culture. 3. **The "Right" Response** - **Ignoring her texts after waking up was justified** because: - You’d already done what she’d asked (sent files, billing info). - You were following medical advice to rest. - Her demands were repetitive and lacked urgency (e.g., asking for data she could access herself). - *Alternative approach (if you wanted to be proactive):* - A short, polite email: *"Hi [Name], I’m still recovering and following my doctor’s advice to rest. I’ve addressed the urgent matters you flagged earlier. Please let me know if there’s anything else critical that requires my attention today."* This sets a boundary while acknowledging her requests. - If she escalates, document the interactions and consider discussing this with a supervisor or HR later. 4. **Long-Term Implications** - **Short-term:** She may see your silence as disrespectful, but her behavior was also unprofessional. If she retaliates (e.g., withholding feedback, making work harder), that’s on *her*. - **Long-term:** This could signal a toxic dynamic. If this pattern continues, it might be worth: - Having a conversation with her about workload expectations. - Reporting the issue to a manager if it affects your health or performance. - Reflecting on whether the firm’s culture supports sustainable work practices. --- ### **Why This Isn’t Just About "Obeying Orders":** Workplaces often glorify "grind culture," but **health > productivity**. Your doctor’s note is a valid reason to prioritize rest—especially when you’ve been overworking for months. Her demands were: - **Repetitive** (she asked for the same things multiple times). - **Unreasonable** (she could’ve done some tasks herself). - **Timing was poor** (while you were sick and recovering). --- ### **Final Verdict: 1 (Not AITA)** You weren’t obligated to respond to her texts when you were unwell, especially after complying with her earlier requests. **Her behavior was boundary-crossing**, and your silence was a reasonable way to protect your health and mental space. That said, this is a great opportunity to: 1. **Advocate for yourself** (e.g., set clearer boundaries in the future). 2. **Reflect on the firm’s culture**—if this is common, it may be worth exploring other opportunities where work-life balance is prioritized. --- ### **Additional Thoughts:** - If you’re worried about backlash, you might frame your silence as *"I’m still recovering and will respond when I’m able"* in an email later. This keeps it professional while reinforcing your limits. - Consider whether this firm values its employees’ well-being. If not, it might be time to reassess your long-term fit. You’re not wrong for putting your health first—especially when others aren’t respecting your limits. Stay strong! 💪
